I.A.3: Name what makes AI need its own governance approach
I.A.4: Recognize and apply the responsible-AI principles

html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Define AI and tell its main types apart
  • Separate an AI model, an AI system and a general-purpose AI model
  • Name the harms and risks AI poses to people, groups, organizations and society
  • Explain the characteristics that make AI need its own governance
  • Apply the common principles of responsible AI and see where they conflict

2I.A.1: Define AI and tell its main types apart

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Know, so the depth is Remember. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Running case

Two Kinds of AI at Helios

  • Lucia Moreno, Head of Talent Acquisition, owns the hiring tool: it predicts which applicants fit a role
  • Anika Berg, Customer Support director, owns the assistant: it generates answers to customer questions
  • Samira Haddad asks whether these are the same kind of AI, and what can go wrong with each
  • Your answers set the scope of the governance program

Defining AI: Four Sources, One Core Beyond the BoK

  • Core idea: a machine-based (engineered) system that, for given objectives, generates outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions
  • OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) and EU AI Act: objectives may be explicit or implicit; the system infers how to produce outputs from its input; levels of autonomy and adaptiveness vary (Article 3(1))
  • NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology): adapted from the OECD and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) wording; outputs influence real or virtual environments
  • ISO/IEC 22989: an engineered system for human-defined objectives (depth marked: from the standard's public summaries)

Exam tip

The wording differs, but a question about the definition asks for the shared core: a system that generates outputs for objectives.

Types of AI: Nested Families

  • AI is the broad field: systems that perform tasks that normally need human intelligence
  • Rule-based systems follow rules people wrote; they are AI in the broad sense but do not learn
  • Machine learning learns patterns from data instead of following written rules
  • Deep learning is machine learning with many-layered neural networks, behind most vision and language models
  • Generative AI creates new content; many such systems are foundation models

Exam tip

If a question asks which is the broadest term, the answer is AI; machine learning is one way of building it.

How Machines Learn: Three Approaches

Approach Learns from Typical output Example
Supervised labeled examples a label or a value scoring an application as a fit or not a fit
Unsupervised unlabeled data groups, patterns, outliers grouping customers; spotting unusual transactions
Reinforcement rewards for actions a way of acting a robot or game player improving by trial
  • Self-supervised learning builds labels from the data itself; it trains many large language models
  • Labels cost effort and can carry human bias, which is why they matter to governance
Exam tip

Labels point to supervised learning, no labels to unsupervised, rewards to reinforcement.

Predictive, Generative and Agentic AI

Kind What it does Helios example
Predictive scores, classifies or forecasts from past data the hiring tool ranks applicants
Generative creates new text, images, audio or code the assistant writes answers
Agentic pursues a goal by planning and acting with tools, with few human steps a proposed function that books meetings itself
  • Narrow AI is built for specific tasks; artificial general intelligence would match people across tasks and is a goal, not what today's laws regulate
  • More autonomy means more need for human oversight (modules 10 and 13)
Exam tip

Do not confuse general-purpose AI (a legal term for breadth of use) with general AI (human-level ability).

AI Model, AI System, General-Purpose AI Beyond the BoK

  • An AI model is the trained component: the learned patterns that turn input into output
  • An AI system puts a model to work with data flows, an interface, rules and a purpose
  • General-purpose AI model (Article 3(63)): shows significant generality, is competent at a wide range of distinct tasks, and can be built into many downstream systems
  • General-purpose AI system (Article 3(66)): a system based on such a model that can serve a variety of purposes
  • Helios: the Corvid Labs model is a general-purpose model; the support assistant built on it is an AI system

Exam tip

Law and standards often attach duties to the system, and some, such as the general-purpose AI rules in module 6, to the model.

The AI Life Cycle Frames the Whole Exam

  • Stages: plan and design, collect data, build and train, test and validate, release, deploy and use, monitor and maintain, retire
  • Domain III governs development as the developer sees it; domain IV governs deployment and use as the deployer sees it
  • Risks and duties differ by stage, so policies are written stage by stage (module 3)
  • Governance does not stop at release: monitoring and retirement belong to the life cycle

Exam tip

When a question names a stage, ask who acts at that stage: the developer or the deployer.

3I.A.2: Name the kinds of AI risk and harm and who bears them

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Identify, so the depth is Understand. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Who Gets Hurt: People, Groups, Organizations, Society

  • Individuals: a wrongly rejected application, loss of privacy, physical or psychological harm, lost economic opportunity
  • Groups: discrimination against a sub-group, stereotyping
  • Organizations: disrupted operations, security breaches, monetary loss, damaged reputation
  • Society: weakened democratic participation, unequal access to education, disinformation at scale
  • NIST also counts harm to ecosystems: connected systems, supply chains, natural resources and the environment

Exam tip

Name who bears the harm first; the category follows from the victim.

Types of Risk: Misalignment, Ethics and Bias, Complexity and Scale

Risk type What it means Helios example
Misalignment with objectives the system optimizes something other than what people intended the hiring tool learns to favor the style of past hires, not job performance
Ethics and bias risk unfair, discriminatory or intrusive outcomes one group of applicants scores lower for reasons unrelated to the job
Complexity and scalability the system is hard to understand and test, and one flaw repeats at volume the same flaw touches every one of about 12,000 applications a quarter
Exam tip

Misalignment means the objective the system really pursues differs from the objective the organization meant to give it.

Generative AI Adds Its Own Risks Beyond the BoK

  • NIST's generative-AI profile names twelve risks unique to or made worse by generative AI
  • Confabulation: confident, false output (often called hallucination)
  • Data privacy: leakage or unauthorized use of personal or sensitive data
  • Intellectual property: easier copying or replication of protected content
  • Information integrity: deepfakes and disinformation at scale
  • The rest include harmful bias, over-reliance on the system, security, environmental cost and opaque supply chains

Exam tip

Hallucination is the popular name; the NIST term is confabulation.

4I.A.3: Name what makes AI need its own governance approach

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Identify, so the depth is Understand. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Why AI Needs Its Own Governance Approach

  • Traditional software: logic written by people; the same input gives the same output
  • AI: patterns learned from data; outputs are probabilities and can vary
  • A software failure is a bug to find and fix; an AI failure is an error rate to manage
  • AI behavior can drift as data change, so maintenance never ends
  • Testing is statistical, on samples, because no checklist can cover every input

Exam tip

Deterministic versus probabilistic output is the contrast the BoK itself names.

Seven Characteristics That Change Governance

  • Complexity: many components and parameters, hard to reason about
  • Opacity: hard to see why a given output was produced
  • Autonomy: acts with little or no human step
  • Speed and scale: decisions in volume, so errors multiply
  • Potential for harm or misuse: powerful tools can be turned to bad ends
  • Data dependency: system quality follows data quality
  • Probabilistic outputs: likelihoods, not certainties

Exam tip

A question may give a symptom and ask for the characteristic; match the symptom to the one-line meaning.

From Characteristic to Governance Response

Characteristic What governance adds
Complexity documentation, expert review, staged testing
Opacity explainability methods, model documentation, disclosure
Autonomy human oversight, limits on what the system may do
Speed and scale monitoring, thresholds, a way to stop the system
Potential for harm or misuse risk assessment, use restrictions, access control
Data dependency data governance, quality and provenance checks
Probabilistic outputs error-rate targets, confidence information, review of edge cases
Exam tip

The governance response follows from the characteristic: opacity calls for explanation, autonomy for oversight.

5I.A.4: Recognize and apply the responsible-AI principles

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Identify, so the depth is Understand. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

Responsible AI: The Common Principles Beyond the BoK

  • Fairness: are people treated equitably?
  • Safety and reliability: does it work as intended without harm?
  • Privacy and security: are people's data and the system protected?
  • Transparency and explainability: can people see and understand it?
  • Accountability: who answers for the outcome?
  • Human-centricity: does it serve human rights, agency and well-being?
  • Sources use different lists (the OECD five principles, the EU's seven ethical principles in Recital 27, NIST's seven characteristics) but overlap heavily

Exam tip

Learn the common core, not one source's list; the BoK asks for the principles that recur.

Fairness and the Kinds of Bias Beyond the BoK

Kind of bias Where it comes from Helios example
Systemic institutions, norms and society, reflected in data and processes past hiring favored some groups, and old résumés carry that pattern
Computational and statistical non-representative samples, flawed measurement or modeling training data hold few applicants from a new region
Human-cognitive how people read and use AI output recruiters accept the score without question (automation bias)
  • NIST names these three categories; each can occur without any intent to discriminate
  • Removing bias does not by itself make a system fair: fairness differs across cultures and uses
  • Test fairness for the context, then document the choice
Exam tip

Match the example to the source: society and process is systemic, unrepresentative data is statistical, people over-trusting output is cognitive.

Safety, Reliability, Privacy and Security

  • Safety: the system does not endanger people, property or the environment, in intended use or in foreseeable misuse
  • Reliability: it performs as intended and consistently, including on inputs it did not see in training (robustness)
  • Privacy: people keep control of their personal data; collect and infer only what is needed (AI can infer private facts)
  • Security: the system, model and data are protected from attack, theft and misuse
  • The pairs overlap: an insecure model is also unreliable, and a privacy leak can become a security incident
Exam tip

Safety and reliability ask whether it works without harm; privacy and security ask whether the data and the system are protected.

Transparency, Explainability and Interpretability

  • Transparency: what happened in the system, and what information about it is available
  • Explainability: how a decision was made, the mechanisms behind the operation
  • Interpretability: why, and what the output means in its context for the user
  • The three support each other; risk from poor explanation is managed by describing how the system works for the user's role and skill
  • Helios: applicants are told AI is used (transparency); the recruiter sees which factors drove a score (explainability); the recruiter understands what the score means for the role (interpretability)

Exam tip

What happened, how, why: that order is transparency, explainability, interpretability.

Accountability and Human-Centricity

  • Accountability: named people answer for each stage and each outcome; it is not left to the model or the vendor
  • It needs documentation, decision records, escalation paths and the ability to audit
  • Human-centricity: AI serves people and respects human rights, agency and well-being
  • Human oversight is often described in three forms: a person decides (in the loop), monitors and can intervene (on the loop) or controls whether and how the system is used (in command)
  • Helios: a recruiter reviews every rejection the tool recommends, and Samira Haddad is the accountable executive
Exam tip

A vendor contract can share tasks, but it does not move accountability away from the organization that uses the system.

When Principles Pull Apart: Trade-offs Beyond the BoK

  • NIST gives three examples: predictive accuracy versus interpretability, interpretability versus privacy, and privacy-enhancing techniques versus accuracy when data are sparse
  • Analysis can show that a trade-off exists, not how to resolve it
  • The resolution depends on the context and values, and should be transparent and justified
  • Helios: a more accurate hiring model that cannot explain its ranking against a simpler model that can

Exam tip

The right answer to a trade-off question is rarely to always pick one principle; it is to decide by context and document why.

6Exam Q&A

6.1 Practice questions (one best answer, or select exactly the number the question asks for)

S1Which feature do the OECD, EU AI Act and NIST definitions of an AI system have in common?

  • AThe system must learn its own rules from labeled training examples supplied by people
  • BThe system generates outputs, such as predictions or decisions, for given objectives
  • CThe system must make its final decisions without a person reviewing them afterwards
  • DThe system must be offered for sale as a software product in a commercial market
Show the answer

Answer: B. All three describe a machine-based or engineered system that generates outputs, such as predictions, recommendations, content or decisions, for objectives. None requires labeled training, full autonomy or a market sale; autonomy levels are said to vary.

S2Helios finds that its hiring tool gives lower scores to women than to comparable men. Which TWO harms to people does this show? (Select TWO.)

  • AHarm to an ecosystem, through heavy use of computing resources
  • BHarm to an individual, through lost economic opportunity
  • CHarm to an organization, through disrupted supply chains
  • DHarm to a group, through discrimination against a sub-group
  • EHarm to society, through weakened democratic participation
Show the answer

Answer: B, D. A woman scored down loses a job opportunity, which is harm to an individual's economic opportunity, and the pattern is discrimination against a group. Computing resources, supply chains and democratic participation are different harms that the facts do not show.

S3A team proposes governing a new machine-learning model like any other software release: test it once against a checklist, then leave it unchanged. Which characteristic of AI makes this approach insufficient?

  • AAI source code is harder to store and version than other software, so a separate policy is required
  • BTesting before release is too slow for AI, so teams usually skip it and rely on user feedback
  • CIts outputs are probabilistic and its data can change after release
  • DAI always needs a human to approve every single output before anyone uses it
Show the answer

Answer: C. Because outputs are statistical and data can drift, behavior can change after release, so testing and monitoring must continue. AI can be versioned and tested, and not every output needs human approval.

S4According to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (RMF), which statement correctly separates transparency, explainability and interpretability?

  • ATransparency covers what happened, explainability how it was decided, interpretability why and what it means
  • BTransparency covers why a decision was made, explainability what happened, and interpretability how it was reached
  • CTransparency covers how a decision was reached, explainability why it was made, and interpretability what happened
  • DThe three terms are interchangeable, because each one describes the same property of the system as a whole
Show the answer

Answer: A. NIST describes the three as distinct but mutually supporting: what happened, how a decision was made, and why it was made and what it means in context. The other orders swap the questions, and the terms are not interchangeable.

S5Veridex offers a more accurate ranking model that cannot show why it ranks candidates as it does, and a simpler model that can. Lucia Moreno asks what to do. What is the best answer?

  • AChoose the more accurate model, because predictive performance is the principle that matters most in practice
  • BChoose the simpler model, because fairness requires accepting the less accurate option in hiring
  • CChoose whichever model the vendor has certified, because certification removes the trade-off
  • DWeigh accuracy against interpretability in this context, then document why you chose
Show the answer

Answer: D. Accuracy and interpretability can trade off, and the answer depends on the context and the values at stake, resolved in a transparent and justifiable way. No principle automatically outranks the others, and certification does not remove the trade-off.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
AI a machine-based system that generates outputs for objectives; model, system and general-purpose model are different things
Types machine learning, deep learning, generative and agentic AI; supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning
Harms to individuals, groups, organizations and society; plus generative-AI risks
Why different seven characteristics, from opacity and autonomy to data dependency and probabilistic output
Principles six that recur (fairness, accountability, human-centricity, transparency and explainability, privacy and security, safety and reliability); they can conflict
